me_canada_cliff_rock.blurb: The roped climbing at Canada Cliff, a steep granite wall above Echo Lake in Acadia National Park. Trees shade the face, so it stays cool on summer days and is sheltered from wind later in the year, which makes summer and fall the comfortable seasons. Expect mostly trad lines with a fair number of bolted routes and a few top-rope setups, running from about 5.9 up through 5.12 with the bulk in the 5.10s and 5.11s. The rock is steep and sharp-holded, and seeps and moss from above mean it dries slowly, so the easier lines can stay damp after rain.
me_canada_cliff_rock.parking_note: Use the long Echo Lake beach lot as your starting point.
me_canada_cliff_rock.approach: Walk up the access road from the beach lot to the bus turnaround, climb the wooden steps, then follow a short path of about a fifth of a mile through talus to a faint track that leads up to the base.

me_c_main_face.blurb: The slabby central face of Parks Pond Bluff in the Clifton Crags, a long-time favorite of Maine climbers and the place many of them first meet the bluff. Most of the climbing is low-angle slab, with a good mix of bolted lines and trad routes, and the great majority fall between 5.7 and 5.8, with a handful of harder lines and an easy scramble. Brush can crowd the edges of the face. From the top of the bluff there are views over the pond and the hills around it. A steeper, harder wall sits just to the left.
me_c_main_face.parking_note: A small unsigned grassy pullout beside Route 9, a few miles east of the Route 180 junction and just beyond Parks Pond, holds two or three cars.
me_c_main_face.approach: Two short unmarked trails split from the pullout: one heads to the top of the bluff, the other to the base of the face, roughly a third of a mile.

me_high_meadow_wall.blurb: The main upper cliff of the Shell Pond crags in western Maine, set in forest near Evans Notch. The wall is steep to overhanging and the climbing is almost all bolted, concentrated in the 5.11s and 5.12s with some 5.10. Lots of lines end partway up the wall, which makes rigging from above awkward, and anchors are two-bolt rappel stations; a 60 m rope serves for most descents. A few lines stay climbable in drizzle. In winter the lower tier is known for sunny ice.

md_cliff_trail_boulders.blurb: A cluster of boulders in a clearing beside the Cliff Trail in Cunningham Falls State Park, in the Catoctin hills. Problems run from V0 to V8, with the middle grades dominating and plenty of V2 and V4. Most of the problems sit on the largest boulder, Jonah, with smaller blocks nearby that add variety. The first boulder you reach as you climb the trail is Flying Squirrel. Pack out your chalk and trash, since the blocks sit beside a popular hiking trail.
md_cliff_trail_boulders.approach: Take the upper, yellow-blazed Cliff Trail uphill for a few hundred feet to the clearing holding the boulders.

md_highlands.blurb: A bouldering zone up on Elk Ridge behind Maryland Heights, above the Potomac near Harpers Ferry. The rock is hard quartzite with good edges and cracks, and the Highlands are almost entirely boulder problems, with plenty of easy and moderate lines from VB through V5 and only a few harder ones. Big Dipper, a jug traverse beneath a low roof, is a standout. The Tiers, a slabby area, sits downhill. The forest hides some blocks, and they grow over in summer.

md_balcony_rock.blurb: A quartzite crag on Elk Ridge just west of Sandy Hook, across the Potomac from Harpers Ferry. The wall is clean, dense and vertical, reaching around 80 feet, with a roof crack and a flake among its features. Most roped climbing is trad and top-rope between about 5.7 and 5.11, and the boulders at its base see more traffic than the wall, mostly V1 to V8 problems. The top has a nice view. Balcony Jr. and the Highlands boulders lie close by.

md_south_bank_pipeline_area.blurb: The largest cluster of boulders on the south bank of Northwest Branch, a wooded stream corridor minutes north of Washington, DC. Problems are spread across every grade from V0 into the double digits, with the heart of it in the V3 to V7 range, and the sub-areas include Nice Slot, Muddy Jugs and Heavens. Families and hikers pass through on weekends, so the holds are wearing smooth in places. Brush sand off shoes and chalk off holds, and bring a spotter, since some blocks are close to the water.

md_fisherman_s.blurb: A bouldering area along Morgan Run in Patapsco State Park's Morgan Run Natural Environment Area, in Carroll County. Several tall formations on the stream bank offer highball potential, and a few can also be top-roped. Problems run from VB into the double digits, mainly V0 to V5, with V2 the most common grade. Other visitors share the corridor, including anglers and hikers. A path leads from the parking lot across the road to the first boulders.
md_fisherman_s.approach: Cross the road from the parking lot and follow the Fisherman's path to the first boulders.
